analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers deduct half their capital gains, adjust asset costs for inflation, and deduct home-sale losses.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have roughly halved the tax on capital gains, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 9, 1995 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let individuals and corporations deduct 50 percent of their net capital gains from taxable income, cutting the effective tax on long-term gains to roughly 17.5 to 19.8 percent [S2, S3]. It would also have let sellers of stock and business property inflate the original purchase price for inflation, so only real gains above inflation were taxed [S2, S3]. A smaller provision would have given homeowners an itemized deduction for losses when selling a principal residence for less than they paid [S2, S3]. The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there with no action of any kind for two years [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations with large capital gains — a group concentrated at the top of the income scale — would pay far less tax when selling appreciated stock or business property [S2, S3]. Mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, and S corporations would pass the new indexing benefit through to their investors [S3]. Homeowners who must sell a residence for less than they paid would gain a new deduction [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Allows a 50 percent income-tax deduction for net capital gains of both corporate and noncorporate taxpayers, cutting the effective top rate on long-term gains to roughly 17.5–19.8 percent (with conforming withholding rates lowered from 35 percent to 17.5–19.8 percent) [S2, S3].
Requires indexing of the adjusted basis of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year, using the GDP price deflator, so inflation-driven gains are not taxed [S2, S3].
Allows an itemized deduction for losses arising from the sale or exchange of a principal residence [S2, S3].

Passes the indexing benefit through regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, S corporations, and common trust funds, letting fund investors get the adjustment without selling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, through the lost revenue from a large cut in capital gains taxation and from inflation-adjusted basis on appreciated assets; over time that revenue shortfall must be made up by other taxpayers or by borrowing. Because capital gains are reported overwhelmingly by the highest-income households, the tax cut itself would flow mainly to them while the offsetting burden would fall broadly.

drawbacks.text: The 50 percent deduction and inflation indexing would sharply reduce federal revenue, since gains on stocks and business property held over a year — the largest pool of capital gains — would be taxed at roughly half the previous effective rate or escape tax entirely where gains merely matched inflation [S2, S3].

The benefit is concentrated: capital gains are reported mostly by the wealthiest households, so the largest dollar benefits would go to those with the biggest appreciated portfolios, while the revenue cost is shared by everyone.

The new home-sale loss deduction would raise valuation and enforcement questions — a homeowner selling to a relative or associate could claim a paper loss — and it would mostly help sellers in down markets, doing nothing for owners in normal times.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a large, permanent tax cut aimed at gains from stocks and business assets, which are concentrated among the highest earners, financed by the Treasury and ultimately by everyone else. Supporters argued lower taxes on gains would encourage investment and job creation — the bill's own title and stated purpose [S3] — but the text contains no revenue offset, so the cost would show up as deficits or higher taxes elsewhere. The one broadly shared benefit, the home-sale loss deduction, is narrow and helps only sellers caught in a falling market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on January 9, 1995, with introductory remarks and one Republican cosponsor [S1, S4, S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind [S1, S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the tax code stayed exactly as it was: holders of large capital gains got no new tax cut, and the Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have given up. Homeowners selling at a loss also kept nothing, since that provision died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury; capital-gains holders got no new cut

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on January 9, 1995.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Bob Packwood
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Finance Committee during the period the bill sat without any committee action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; its only recorded support was its Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, and no member ever had to vote for or against it [S1, S4, S5].

industries.industry: Investors in stocks and business assets (highest-income households)
industries.note: The bill would halve the effective tax on their long-term gains and remove tax on gains that merely match inflation, a benefit that scales with the size of the portfolio. The revenue cost would fall on the Treasury and ultimately on other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill gives regulated investment companies and REITs special pass-through of the new indexing benefit and lets REITs avoid frequent asset revaluation, making their products more tax-advantaged [S3]. Ordinary savers in those funds would share some benefit, but the tax preference flows mainly to larger investors.
Lower tax on trading gains and inflation-indexed basis would increase the after-tax return on securities transactions, encouraging more trading activity that generates commissions and fees.

The 50 percent deduction and indexing apply to corporate taxpayers as well as individuals, cutting tax on corporate gains from asset sales [S2, S3]. The bill simultaneously repeals the separate 50 percent exclusion for small-business stock gains, replacing a targeted break with a broad one [S3].

The bill would allow an itemized deduction for losses on selling a principal residence, helping owners forced to sell in a down market [S2, S3]. This is the bill's one provision aimed squarely at ordinary households.
